title: 第四章　受审的知识分子：齐娜伊达·德尼谢夫斯卡娅

children: 1917年秋天布尔什维克夺取政权时，齐娜伊达·德尼谢夫斯卡娅（Zinaida Denisevskaya）是沃罗涅日的一名30岁的学校教师，那里是俄罗斯农业腹地的一个省会。在她的日记中，她对新政权几乎没有好话：“布尔什维克的胜利让我担忧和恐惧。我不信任他们。他们既不诚实也不聪明；我不是在说例外情况，但总体而言，他们愚昧而邪恶。”

Zinaida Denisevskaya was a 30-year-old schoolteacher in Voronezh, a provincial capital in Russia’s agricultural heartland, when the Bolsheviks came to power in the fall of 1917. In her diary she had few favorable words for the new regime: “The Bolshevik victory worries and frightens me. I don’t trust them. They have neither honesty nor intellect; I’m not talking about the exceptions, but on the whole they are dark and evil.”

不到12年后，德尼谢夫斯卡娅记录了她开始经历的一场转变：“在过去的整整一年里，我不知不觉地成了一个‘社会主义者’，我开始理解共产主义了。”又过了一年，她倾诉道：“在过去的12年里，生活重新教育了我，”以及“直到最近我才开始信任党和国家。”她以前的人生观现在在她看来显得“古怪而荒唐”。德尼谢夫斯卡娅谴责她过去的“无知”，实际上从一名斥责共产党人缺乏文化的老师，转变为一名如饥似渴地学习新生活方式的学生。

Less than twelve years later Denisevskaya recorded a transformation she had begun to undergo: “Over the whole last year I have unconsciously become a ‘socialist,’ I am beginning to understand communism.” Another year later she confided: “Life has reeducated me over the past twelve years,” and “only recently have I come to trust the party and the state.” Her previous outlook on life now appeared to her “bizarre and ridiculous.” Castigating her past “ignorance,” Denisevskaya effectively reverted from a teacher, chiding the Communists’ lack of culture, to a student avidly learning the new forms of life.

德尼谢夫斯卡娅从1900年（当时她是一名13岁的女学生）开始写日记，直到她1933年不幸去世。鉴于其篇幅和自我反思的特质，这是一份非凡的记录。在一个层面上，这本日记记录了一连串的思想和往往令人吃惊的启示，这些启示使德尼谢夫斯卡娅从1917年谴责布尔什维克，转变为在20世纪20年代末拥抱他们——而且是字面意义上的拥抱。但日记起止的日期让我们能以更广阔的视角，审视她在数十年灾难性政治和社会变革——沙俄帝国的瓦解、革命的动荡，以及一个致力于重塑人类关系、创造新世界的新政权的最初几年——中不断演进的自我探索。德尼谢夫斯卡娅的自我反思早于苏维埃秩序；她带着成熟且清晰表达的“人格”概念进入了1917年革命。正是从这个视角出发，她批评布尔什维克是没有教养和面目模糊的。然而，多年以后，她却用自己的个人自主权换取了一个看起来无限崇高、宏大且更有意义的价值。通过记录这位女性在政治革命和社会转型的连续过程中，在“个人主义”与“集体主义”两个极端之间对自身所进行的批判性审视，她的日记与那些通常描述集体主义苏联体制侵害公民自主权的叙述大相径庭。

Denisevskaya kept her diary from 1900, when she was a 13-year-old schoolgirl, until her untimely death in 1933. It is an extraordinary record, given its volume and its self-reflective quality. On one level, the journal charts the succession of thoughts and often startling revelations that brought Denisevskaya from condemning the Bolsheviks in 1917 to embracing them—quite literally—by the end of the 1920s. But the framing dates of the diary allow for a broader perspective on her evolving self-exploration across several decades of cataclysmic political and social changes—the breakdown of imperial Russia, the turmoil of revolution, and the early years of a new regime intent on remaking human relationships and creating a new world. Denisevskaya’s self-re-flection predated the Soviet order; she entered the revolution of 1917 with developed and articulated notions of her own “personality.” It was  precisely from this vantage point that she criticized the Bolsheviks as uncultivated and faceless. And yet over the years she came to trade her personal autonomy for a value that appeared infinitely higher, larger, more meaningful. In detailing this woman’s critical engagement of her self between the extreme poles of “individualism” and “collectivism” through a continuum of political revolution and social transformation, her diary differs markedly from customary accounts of the collectivist Soviet system encroaching on the autonomy of its citizens.

德尼谢夫斯卡娅一生都致力于培养自己的人格，从而揭示了她对俄罗斯知识分子精神（ethos）的参与。这一受过教育且具有批判性思维的群体，首先通过致力于创造一个由人格和谐、生活充实、身心完整的人组成的完美社会秩序来定义自身。她对写日记的持续追求，在某种程度上体现了她对这种理想人格类型的持久渴望。从这种长期承诺的角度来看，布尔什维克关于自我的思考和行动方式显得不那么具有原创性，更多是植根于——作为某种变体——对自我修养和自我完善的专注，而这种专注是俄罗斯文化（包括沙俄晚期、革命时期以及苏维埃时期）更广泛阶层所共有的特征。

Throughout her life Denisevskaya retained a commitment to cultivating her personality, thereby revealing her engagement in the ethos of the Russian intelligentsia, that group of educated and critically thinking individuals which defined itself above all by a commitment to the creation of a perfect social order inhabited by harmoniously shaped, fulfilled, and integrated human beings. The continued pursuit of her diary was in some measure an expression of Denisevskaya’s sustained aspiration toward such an ideal type of personality. In light of this longer-term commitment, Bolshevik ways of thinking and acting on the self appear less original, and more situated, as variants of a pre-occupation with working on and perfecting the self that characterized larger segments of Russian culture—late imperial and revolutionary as well as Soviet.

日记中另一个持续的主题，实际上也是其首要主题，就是孤独。多年来，德尼谢夫斯卡娅一直梦想着但从未经历过一段持久的爱情关系（尽管她在晚年曾有过几个月的婚姻）。由于感到不被理解，缺乏开口表达想法的决心，反而不得不听朋友和同事们直言己见，她转而向日记寻求最坚强的“朋友和支持”。甚至在13岁时，她就把自己刻画成一个孤独者，“过于严肃冷静”，且习惯于沉思遐想。当学校里的一个朋友开玩笑地给她起绰号叫“修女”时，她记道：“是的，我是个修女，一个隐士。但这并不是出于我自己的意志才把自己锁在这个窒息的修道院里。”三十年后，在斯大林主义革命的动荡中，在截然不同的条件下，她仍然发出同样的基调：“我正经历着一种最深刻的个人孤独感。”在德尼谢夫斯卡娅多达5623页的惊人日记中，许多（如果不是大部分）篇幅都回荡着她忧郁的声音，这孤独的底色映衬着她对完整和共融的渴望。

Another continuous theme in the diary, and in fact its overriding theme, was loneliness. Over the years Denisevskaya kept dreaming of, but never experienced, a lasting love relationship (though she was married for a few months late in her life). Feeling not understood, lacking the resolve to speak up and being instead subjected to the vocal opinions of her friends and colleagues, she turned to her journal as her strongest “friend and support.” Even as a 13-year-old she cast herself as a loner, “overly serious and calm” and prone to introspective dreaming. When a friend at school jokingly nicknamed her “nun,” she noted: “Yes, I am a nun, a hermit. But it is not out of my own will that I have locked myself in this stifling monastery.” Thirty years later, amid the turmoil of the Stalinist revolution and in starkly different conditions, she still sounded the same tone: “I’m experiencing a most profound sense of personal loneliness.” Of the incredible 5,623 pages of Denisevskaya’s diary writings, many, if not most, resonated with the melancholic sound of her voice, a backdrop of loneliness against which her desires for completion and communality unfolded.

在她的一生中，孤独对德尼谢夫斯卡娅来说意味着很多事情。它部分指代她作为一个未婚女性的困境，但也也包含一种存在层面的孤独，一种在世界上无处遮蔽的感觉。1917年之后，她越来越在阶级的背景下理解她的孤独状态。苏维埃政权热烈宣扬的“劳动集体”概念，向她传达了一种从孤独中解脱出来的承诺，并最终被证明比她对周围粗鲁的共产党人的厌恶更强大。问题仍然在于，她的孤独在多大程度上是一种个人特征（对她最终拥抱苏维埃理想负责），以及在多大程度上孤独是深植于大众和集体崛起时代知识分子的自我形象之中的。

In the course of her life, loneliness meant a variety of things to Denisevskaya. It referred in part to her predicament as an unmarried woman, but it also connoted an existential solitude, a sense of being unsheltered in the world. After 1917 she increasingly came to understand her lonely condition in the context of class. The notion of the “laboring collective,” ardently proclaimed by the Soviet regime, resonated to her with a promise of deliverance from loneliness and eventually proved stronger than her abhorrence of the coarse Communists around her. The question remains to what extent her loneliness was a personal characteristic, responsible for her eventual embrace of the Soviet idea, and to what extent loneliness was ingrained in the intelligentsia’s self-image in an age of rising masses and collectivities.

children: 齐娜伊达·德尼谢夫斯卡娅于1887年出生于沃罗涅日的一个受过教育的精英家庭。她似乎是至少四个孩子中的老大。她的父亲是在她后来就读的一所私立女子学校教科学的老师，且至少曾担任过该校校长。1907年，齐娜伊达考入莫斯科女子高等课程，这是一所成立于1870年代初的大学程度教育机构，在自然科学和人文学科方面提供高水平教育。她主修自然科学。1912年完成学业后，她搬回沃罗涅日，先是在当地中学（gymnasia）和小学担任教师，后来在市图书馆担任馆员。1920年，她离开图书馆，前往沃罗涅日农学院的实验站工作。她在那里度过了余生，与一群农学家合作，实验创新的农业生产和劳动方法，并寻求在当地农民中推广这些方法。

Zinaida Denisevskaya was born in 1887 into a family belonging to Voronezh’s educated elite. She appears to have been the oldest of at least four children. Her father was a science teacher in the private girls’ school which she later attended, and at least at one point he was the director of that school. In 1907 Zinaida enrolled in the Women’s Higher Courses in Moscow, a university-level institution founded in the early 1870s, which provided high-level training in scientific subjects as well as the humanities. She majored in natural sciences. After completing her studies in 1912, she moved back to Voronezh, where she worked first as a teacher in local gymnasia and elementary schools and later as a librarian in the city library. In 1920 she left the library to take up work at the experimental station of the Voronezh Agricultural Institute. She remained there for the rest of her life, working with a team of agronomists who experimented with innovative methods of agricultural production and labor and sought to spread them among the local peasantry.

德尼谢夫斯卡娅在1900年，也就是13岁时开始写日记。她到1919年为止的日记记录保存在五本厚厚的装订本中，每本约有七百页。它们的外观与德尼谢夫斯卡娅记录其苏维埃时期（1919年至1933年）生活的那些薄而脆的笔记本形成了鲜明对比。在她一生的大部分时间里，德尼谢夫斯卡娅经常每天写日记，间隔很少超过一周。许多日记条目一直围绕着相同的主题打转，且带着同样的渴望和宿命论。她将家庭生活描述为充满冲突和不快乐的。虽然齐娜伊达将父亲描绘成温柔慈爱的，但母亲却显得冷酷、严厉且不公。然而，日记也记录了齐娜伊达的母亲在歇斯底里的爆发和对丈夫不忠的麻木痛苦之间交替。

Denisevskaya began keeping a journal in 1900, at the age of 13. Her diary notes of the years up to 1919 are preserved in five thick, bound volumes, each containing about seven hundred pages. Their appearance stands in stark contrast to the thin, brittle notebooks in which Denisevskaya recorded her life in the Soviet period, from 1919 to 1933. For much of her life Denisevskaya wrote diary entries often at daily and rarely at less than weekly intervals. Many of the diary entries keep re-volving around the same themes, and do so with the same yearning and fatalism. She described her family life as conflicted and unhappy. While Zinaida portrayed her father as tender and loving, her mother appeared as cold, harsh, and unjust. Yet the diary also notes Zinaida’s mother alternating between hysterical outbursts and numbed suffering over her husband’s infidelity.

在她早期的日记中，德尼谢夫斯卡娅从未清楚地从社会身份角度定义自己，但她的家庭背景以及她的教育和职业抱负都标志着她是知识分子的一员——如果以服务社会需求的首要道德责任来定义这一群体。这正是她描述父亲的方式：“他完全沉浸在服务社会的想法中，并将自己完全奉献给了它。”女儿渴望自己也成为一名教师，这是1900年代初大多数就读私立中学的俄罗斯女孩共同的目标。成为一名乡村教师并教育“蒙昧”的农民是她们首选的职业，而受过教育的阶层的男孩则想成为医生和科学家。与越来越多同龄的年轻女性一起，齐娜伊达也寻求获得高等教育。像她那一代的其他人一样，她认为大学教育对于“成为一个全面发展的人格、过一种自觉的生活、参与社会生活”至关重要。自由派政治家阿里阿德娜·蒂尔科娃-威廉姆斯（Ariadna Tyrkova-Williams）在回顾她在1880年代的青年时代和道德教育时写道，成为知识分子的一员就是变成一个“具有批判性思维的人，培养理性的世界观”。
如此定义的“人格”不是指任何个人经验性的生活，而是指一个人格（lichnost'）更抽象、更普遍的理念。在进行自我塑造时，知识分子成员试图根据理想化的人性形象来塑造自己。

Nowhere in her early diary did Denisevskaya define herself clearly in social terms, but her family background as well as her educational and professional aspirations marked her as a member of the intelligentsia, if adherence to this group is defined by an overriding moral commitment to serving the needs of society. This was exactly how she described her father: “He is completely preoccupied with his idea to serve society and has given himself completely to it.” The daughter aspired to become a teacher herself, a goal shared by most Russian girls who attended private gymnasia in the early 1900s. To become a village schoolteacher and educate the “dark” peasantry was their profession of choice, whereas boys from the educated classes wanted to become doctors and scientists. Together with an increasing number of young women her age, Zinaida also sought to obtain a higher education. Like others of her generation she saw a university education as essential “to become a fully developed personality, live a conscious life, take part in the life of society.” To become a member of the intelligentsia was to turn into a “critically thinking person, to cultivate a rational worldview,” as the liberal politician Ariadna Tyrkova-Williams wrote, looking back on her youth and moral education in the 1880s.

Personhood, thus defined, referred not to any individual’s empirical life but to a more abstract and general idea of the human personality (lichnost’). In working on themselves, members of the intelligentsia attempted to fashion themselves according to an idealized image of humanity.

这种对发展具有整合世界观的道德人格的承诺，在德尼谢夫斯卡娅的案例中表现得很明显。1904年她17岁时，俄罗斯受过教育的社会中越来越多的阶层开始要求专制政府做出宪法让步。对于这个同情地记录了1905年不断演变的抗议和罢工运动的年轻女性来说，政治领域承诺让她从孤独悲伤的个人生活中逃离，进入一个与同胞共融的欢乐世界。除了追踪“社会日益高涨的热情”外，她还希望把自己铭刻在她所认为的正在崛起的一代人中：“[去]参与整整一代人的重要工作……为了做好准备，我必须阅读，发展自己。”革命成为她发展自己世界观的动力：“我必须向自己澄清我的政治和社会观点，如果还没有，就去构建它们。”“最重要的是形成自己的世界观。可它就是形成不了——完全停滞——苦恼和绝望。”五年后，她仍在抱怨：“我缺乏完整的世界观；因为我无法清晰、合逻辑地向自己解释所有的生活。”

The commitment to the development of a moral personality with an integrated worldview showed well in Denisevskaya’s case. She was 17 in 1904 when ever-larger sections of Russian educated society began to clamor for constitutional concessions from the autocratic government. For this young woman who sympathetically recorded the evolving protest and strike movement of 1905, the political sphere promised an escape from her lonely and sad personal life into a world of joyous communion with fellow citizens. Beyond tracing the “rising enthusiasm of society,” she hoped to inscribe herself into what she perceived as a generation on the rise: “[to] participate in the important work of a whole generation . . . To prepare myself for this I must read, develop.” The revolution served as an impetus for her to develop a worldview of her own: “I must clarify to myself my political and social views, and formulate them if they are not there.” “The main thing is to work out my worldview. But it just won’t be worked out—an absolute standstill—anguish and despair.” Five years later she still complained: “I lack an integral worldview; because I can’t clearly and logically explain all of life to myself.”

然而，虽然革命给了她一种新的共同体归属感（“与一万人一起站在人民宫，我第一次把自己构想成一个人，一个社会成员”），但她觉得站在革命运动的边缘更舒服，在那儿她带着嫉妒和怨恨交织的情绪，关注着她那些活跃在政治舞台上的同龄人的庆祝活动。首先，她抱怨自己身体虚弱，让她只能带着心痛锁在家里，而沃罗涅日的街头“生活正进行得如火如荼”。但大多数活跃在政治上的年轻人都是社会主义者，为她无法支持的激进立场而战。凭借“性格、天性和教育”，她属于“文化改革派”和“渐进派”的党派。“我因此而恨自己。我嫉妒他们，那些勇于冒险和牺牲的年轻人，他们用年轻身体的全部力量生活着。我也对自己感到恼火。”与此同时，她拒绝政党的“狂热和不宽容”，并谴责他们的“没收和杀戮”。她尤其拒绝共产主义意识形态，因为它“完全压制和扼杀了个性”。至于她自己的政治承诺，她认为“教育和人道高于一切。仅做一个有觉悟的无产者是不够的，一个人首先必须是一个人。”

德尼谢夫斯卡娅对政治生活的观察与另一个她开始反思自己作为“人”的领域交织在一起。这就是她的性。这个主题最早出现在1907年2月的一条记录中。在总结了她观看的第一部歌剧《卡门》的热情描述后，她记道，“某些新的东西”正发生在她身上。她对一位29岁的男性朋友变得“轻佻”，她开始不把他看作“一个抽象的存在”，而是作为一个“身体层面的人”：“我又在自己身上看到了那些我试图抹杀的东西，那些我觉得恶心的东西——感官欲望。在我的灵魂深处，我正沉沦于最隐秘、最烦乱的想法和欲望中，我发现我想得到他随意的爱抚。”

And yet, while the revolution provided her with a new sense of community (“standing together with ten thousand people at the People’s Palace, I for the first time conceived of myself as a human being, a member of society”), she felt more comfortable on the sidelines of the revolutionary movement, from where she followed with a mix of envy and resentment the celebrations of her politically active peers. In the first place she blamed her poor health for keeping her locked at home with an aching heart, while down in the streets of Voronezh “life is in full swing.” But most of the politically active youth were socialists and fought for radical positions that she could not bring herself to support. By virtue of “character, nature, and education” she belonged to the party of “cultural reformers” and “gradualists.” “And I hate myself for this. I envy them, the young people who take on risk and sacrifice, who live with all the strength of their young bodies. And I’m annoyed at myself.” At the same time, she rejected the “fanaticism and intolerance” of political parties and condemned their “expropriations and killings.” She particularly rejected Communist ideology, which “completely suppresses and smothers individuality.” As for her own political commitments, she valued “education and humaneness above everything else. It’s not enough to be a conscious proletarian, one must first and foremost be a human being.”

Denisevskaya’s observations on political life intersected with another sphere in which she began to reflect on herself as a “human being.” This was her sexuality. The theme first surfaced in an entry for February 1907. In concluding a glowing account of the first opera she had ever attended—Carmen—she noted that “something new” was happening to her. She was becoming “flirtatious” toward a 29-year-old male friend, to whom she was beginning to relate not as “an abstract being,” but as a “physical person”: “Again I see in myself that which I am trying to kill off, that which I find disgusting—sensuality. In my soul I am sinking to the most hidden and disturbed thoughts and desires, I see that I want casual caresses from him.”

在1905年抗议活动之后，整个俄罗斯阅读界出现了一种对本能和性的新痴迷，这只能部分由新闻改革和随后的小报崛起解释。这种关注点不在于性本身，而在于附着其上的自我实现的主张。这场令受过教育的社会舆论极化数年之久的辩论中心，是米哈伊尔·阿尔齐巴舍夫（Mikhail Artsybashev）的情色小说《萨宁》（Sanin，1907年连载出版），书中那位风流成性的同名主人公说服他引诱的女性，性冲动是提升而非降低了她们的人格。影响力仅次于《萨宁》的是另一部小说，阿纳斯塔西娅·韦尔比茨卡娅（Anastasia Verbitskaya）的《幸福之钥》（Keys to Happiness），它更专门针对女性读者。女主人公玛尼娅追求一种结合了个人自主、职业成功、爱情和性的生活方式。她从一个男人那里学到，女性可以而且应该允许自己享受身体快乐，而不必成为爱情的奴隶，个人自主和没有情感纠葛的性满足构成了“幸福之钥”。

Throughout the Russian reading world there appeared a new obsession with instinct and sexuality in the wake of the 1905 protests that could be only partly explained by the press reforms and the ensuing rise of the boulevard press. The preoccupation was not with sexuality as such but with the claims to self-realization that were attached to it. At the center of a debate that polarized the opinion of educated society for several years was Mikhail Artsybashev’s erotic novel Sanin (published in installments in 1907), whose philandering eponymous hero convinces the women he seduces that sexual impulses improve rather than degrade their personalities. Secondary only to Sanin in influence was another novel, Anastasia Verbitskaya’s Keys to Happiness, which more specifically addressed a female audience. Its heroine, Manya, pursues a way of life that combines personal autonomy, professional success, love, and sexuality. She learns from a man that women can and should allow themselves physical pleasure without becoming slaves of love, that personal autonomy and sexual satisfaction without emotional involvement constitute “the keys to happiness.”

当时的批评家将这些小说的出现视为文化剧变的征兆。自1860年代以来由激进知识分子传播的革命斗争和为社会牺牲自我的精神，在失败的革命背景下似乎信誉扫地。当时青年被视为知识分子的接班人，他们对社会和政治的责任感正在减弱。革命运动的集体力量和道德标准正消散为低下的个人主义欲望。萨宁是典型的反英雄，与过去激励知识分子的自我牺牲的地下战士截然相反。他是一个极端的个人主义者，为了满足他的“自然”需求而生活，鄙视社会道德和政治。最令人震惊的不是萨宁的自由恋爱观念——毕竟车尔尼雪夫斯基在1860年代就主张过三人行——而是性与社会解放议程的脱钩，并将其宣告为最高的目标本身。《幸福之钥》和《萨宁》无疑都只是1900年代和1910年代俄罗斯和欧洲文化中个人主义和主体性趋势的象征性表达。这一趋势受尼采思想（阿尔齐巴舍夫承认受其影响）和新康德主义哲学的影响，也受到专制政府改革政策的影响，尤其是首相斯托雷平（Stolypin）对“强有力的农民”的倚重以及解散农村公社的决定。

Contemporary critics apprehended the appearance of these novels as an indication of a cultural sea change. The ethos of revolutionary struggle and self-sacrifice for society, propagated by the radical intelligentsia since at least the 1860s, seemed discredited in light of the failed revolution. Social and political commitments were eroding among contemporary youth, the designated heirs of the intelligentsia. The collective strength and the moral standards of the revolutionary movement were dissipating into base individualistic urges. Sanin was the antihero par excellence, an opposite of the self-sacrificing underground fighter who had inspired the intelligentsia in the past. He was an extreme individualist, who lived in order to satisfy his “natural” needs and despised social morality and politics. Most shocking was not Sanin’s notion of free love—after all, Chernyshevsky had advocated a ménage à trois back in the 1860s—but the disconnection of sexuality from an agenda of social emancipation and its proclamation as a highest goal in itself. Both The Keys to Happiness and Sanin, to be sure, were only symbolic expressions of a trend toward individualism and subjectivity in Russian and European culture of the 1900s and 1910s. It was a trend marked by Nietzschean ideas (which Artsybashev acknowledged as an influence) and neo-Kantian philosophy, but also by the reform policies of the autocratic government, notably Prime Minister Stolypin’s wager on the “strong peasant” and the decision to break up the peasant commune.

德尼谢夫斯卡娅采用了这种新的文学个人主义语言来进行自我分析。在日记中反思她与几位男性朋友的关系时，她思索自己是否在生活中充分地“表达了自己”。“在个人生活中，我是独立的和个人主义的吗？”对这些朋友来说，她是平等独立的伙伴，还是成了他们的“奴隶”？德尼谢夫斯卡娅总结道，即便外表看起来是顺从的，她也必须忠于自我：“我不能允许我的灵魂被侵犯。”离开沃罗涅日去莫斯科学习后，她与一个在日记中仅被称为“那个学生”的男人有了往来。她对他的描述围绕着学生运动最迫切的问题展开：它是否仍是一股进步力量，还是已被新的个人主义致命地腐蚀了？德尼谢夫斯卡娅的诊断令人清醒。显然，这段恋情中有她喜欢的一面：“我喜欢他的手划过我的肩膀和乳房……从未有人这样爱抚过我。人们会喜欢或崇拜我，把我放在神坛上，他们会爱抚我的灵魂，但不是我的肉体。甚至我的母亲也没有爱抚过她的女儿。现在当他爱抚我时，感觉很好。”但她也深陷道德顾虑：“那个学生”教育她感官的任务是否贬低了她的人格？她的一部分想撇开这些疑虑。毕竟，她理想中的女性不是歌德《浮士德》中的玛格丽特，也不是屠格涅夫《贵族之家》中的丽莎——那些顺从、贞洁的女性，男性的被动受害者——而是一个现代的、自我肯定的、社会活跃且坚定的个人，就像车尔尼雪夫斯基笔下的薇拉·帕夫洛夫娜，或屠格涅夫另一部小说《前夜》中的叶琳娜。“她们都生活过、恋爱过、了解过男人，这并没有丝毫玷污她们，相反，新的复杂体验提升了她们每个人的人格，使其得到发展。”通过这些作为几代俄罗斯年轻女性个人和社会行为楷模的文学女主人公，德尼谢夫斯卡娅坚持她表达性本能的个人权利，并将这种自我肯定与当时的进步价值观——“个人主义”和“每个人的个人自由”——联系起来。

Denisevskaya took up the language of the new literary individualism for the purposes of her own self-analysis. Reflecting in her diary on her relationships with several male friends, she wondered whether she had sufficiently “expressed herself in life. Was I independent and individualist in my personal life?” Was she an equal and independent partner to these friends, or had she become their “slave”? Even if outwardly she appeared submissive, Denisevskaya concluded, she had to remain true to herself: “I cannot allow my soul to be violated.” After leaving Voronezh to study in Moscow, she became involved with a man who in the diary is called merely “the student.” Her description of him was embedded in the most burning question about the student movement: Was it still a progressive force, or had it been fatally corrupted by the new individualism? Denisevskaya’s diagnosis was sobering. Clearly there were sides to the affair that she enjoyed: “I like it when he slides his hand over my shoulders and breasts . . . Nobody has ever caressed me like this. People would like or admire me, put me on a pedestal, they would caress my soul, but not my body. Even my mother did not caress her little girl. And now it feels good when he caresses me.” But she was beset by moral qualms: Had “the student’s” mission to educate her senses degraded her as a person? Part of her wanted to brush aside these doubts. Her ideal woman, after all, was not Faust’s Gretchen, or Turgenev’s Liza (from A House of Gentlefolk)—submissive, virtuous women, passive victims of men—but a modern, self-affirming, socially active and committed individual, like Chernyshevsky’s Vera Pavlovna, or like Elena, from another of Turgenev’s novels (On the Eve). “They all lived, loved, and knew men, which did not taint them in the least, on the contrary, new complex experiences raised the personality of each of them, made it develop.” With these literary heroines, who served as models of personal and social behavior for generations of young Russian women, Denisevskaya insisted on her personal right to express her sexual instincts, and she linked this self-affirmation to progressive values of the day—“individualism” and “individual freedom for everybody.”

然而，这种个人主义和唯物主义的自我定义是否能与齐娜伊达的知识分子背景及其对道德定义的“人格”概念的承诺调和，仍有待观察。她不得不承认，车尔尼雪夫斯基和屠格涅夫小说中的女主人公在1905年后道德萧条的学生运动氛围中并非可行的榜样。薇拉·帕夫洛夫娜所倡导的作为社会进步理想的自由恋爱，一旦脱离了社会目标，就会合乎逻辑地堕落为盲目的生理冲动。这种赤裸裸的个人主义不是解放，而是贬低。德尼谢夫斯卡娅描述了在她进行萨宁式的实验过程中，她的道德自我如何成了身体的囚犯。支撑她将自己定义为“人”（chelovek）和有“人格”的人（lichnost'）的道德人文主义，使她无法完全接受她的本能是她人类“本性”表达的观点，因为那会把她降低为一只“动物”。最后，她对那个冒充她的“‘人生导师’”但仅仅唤醒了她“女人的本能”，然后离开她“冷漠地”回到妻儿身边的学生只感到苦涩。在德尼谢夫斯卡娅的词汇中，“女人”一词带有明显的负面色彩，暗示着身体本能、非理性和低级阴谋的艺术：“我变得更有经验了，我学会了在感情上撒谎和欺骗。我不再是一个真诚的小女孩，我开始理解我作为女人的力量和角色。”做一个“女人”就是按性的方式去感受和行动——这与自觉的、道德的“人类”意志形成了鲜明对比。在某些方面，德尼谢夫斯卡娅对“女人”的理解与她对政治领域的表现相似：两者都是受激情和自私利益支配的领域，与更高、更普遍的“人性”和“社会”领域相对立。

It remained to be seen, however, whether this individualist and materialist definition of the self could be reconciled with Zinaida’s intelligentsia background and her commitment to a morally defined notion of “personality.” The heroines from Chernyshevsky’s and Turgenev’s novels, she had to recognize, were not viable role models in the morally depressed climate of the post-1905 student movement. The free love advocated by Vera Pavlovna as a socially progressive ideal logically degenerated into blind physiological impulses as soon as it was divested of a social purpose. Such naked individualism was not emancipating, but debasing. Denisevskaya described how in the course of her Saninlike experiments her moral self became a prisoner of her body. The moral humanism underpinning her self-definition as a human being (chelovek) and as a person (lichnost’) made it impossible for her to fully accept the idea that her instincts were expressions of her human “nature,” for that would reduce her to an “animal.” In the end she felt nothing but bitterness toward the student who had posed as her “‘teacher of life,’” but had aroused in her merely “the instinct of a woman,” then had left her and “indifferently” returned to his wife and children. “Woman” in Denisevskaya’s vocabulary had a decidedly negative ring, connoting bodily instincts, irrationality, and the art of lowly intrigue: “I have become more experienced, I have learned to lie and be deceptive about my feelings. I’m no longer a sincere little girl, I have come to understand my power and role as a woman.” To be a “woman” was to feel and act sexually—in marked contrast to the conscious and moral “human” will. In some ways, Denisevskaya’s understanding of “woman” was analogous to her representation of the political sphere: both were realms governed by passions and selfish interests, in opposition to the higher, universal spheres of “humanity” and “society.”

德尼谢夫斯卡娅在俄罗斯女性主义者亚历山德拉·柯伦泰（Alexandra Kollontai）一篇题为《新女性》的文章中发现了综合她对“女人”和“人”的理解的可能性。写于1913年的文章中，柯伦泰宣布一种新型女性作为一种社会事实出现了：年轻的女工和办公室职员，现代经济生活的产物，正大量出现在俄罗斯和国外。她们在物质上自食其力且自信，在法律上单身，在心理上独立自由。她们与“旧时代的女性”相对立，后者只是丈夫的附属品，是客体而非主体。现代女性反抗她传统的“丧失个性的顺从”地位。这种反叛的姿态迫使“新女性”走向孤独，因为她不能指望那些只想占有她、从而将她客体化的男人的真爱。目前男人能给她的只有生理上的满足，而她的自我实现必须通过工作和公共服务来实现。然而，她知道，在未来的某个遥远时刻，拥有“不同灵魂配置”的人（指男人）将会出现。他们将能够体验并给予真正的、同志般的爱，这种爱不以客体化女性为代价。

德尼谢夫斯卡娅写道，在读完这篇文章后，她开始“理解”自己是一个“新女性”。她可以过一种社会和道德上有意义的生活，而不必压制她的本能欲望。这个模式之所以吸引人，不仅因为它将生理与道德结合在一起，显得新颖而进步，还因为它为她作为单身、孤独的年轻女性的处境提供了一种解释。柯伦泰引用的一位文学女主人公写了一本日记，其中的孤独主题与德尼谢夫斯卡娅自己的记录如出一辙：“我习惯了孤独，但今天我觉得如此寂寞……这是否意味着我不独立、不自由？我太孤独了。”在评论这本日记时，柯伦泰自信地为女主人公的折磨提供了解决方案：“难道我们在这抱怨中没有听到一个习惯于被熟悉且心爱的声音包围、习惯于感受到某人习惯性爱抚的旧时代女性的声音吗？”柯伦泰的新女性坚决抵制这种传统渴望：“她离开了，分手时对他静静地微笑，她去寻找她的幸福之梦，她走着，带着她自己的灵魂，仿佛……她有必要为自己建立一种新的生活。”在这种解读中，孤独与其说是一种诅咒，不如说是一种成就，是作为现代女性实现自我的第一步。

Denisevskaya discovered the possibility of synthesizing her understanding of “woman” and “human being” in an article by the Russian feminist Alexandra Kollontai entitled “The New Woman.” Writing in 1913, Kollontai proclaimed the emergence of a new type of woman as a social fact: young female workers and office employees, products of modern economic life who were appearing in large numbers in Russia and abroad. They were materially self-reliant and assertive, legally single, and psychologically independent and free. They stood in opposition to the “woman of the past” who was a mere appendix to her husband, an object rather than a subject. The modern woman fought against her traditional position of “impersonal submissiveness.” Her defiant outlook forced the “new woman” into loneliness, as she could not expect to be truly loved by men who only wanted to possess and thus objectify her. All that men could offer her for now was physiological satisfaction, while her self-realization was to occur through work and public service. Yet she knew that at some distant point in the future people (meaning men) with a “different configuration of the soul” would appear. They would be able to experience and dispense true, comradely love, which did not entail the objectification of women.

In reading this article, Denisevskaya wrote, she came to “understand” herself as a “new woman.” She could lead a socially and morally meaningful life without having to repress her instinctual desires. The model was attractive not only because it married physiology to morality and appeared new and progressive but also because it provided an explanation for her plight as a single and lonely young woman. One of the literary heroines cited by Kollontai kept a diary which sounded the theme of loneliness familiar from Denisevskaya’s own record: “I’m used to being alone, but today I feel so lonely . . . Does this mean that I’m not independent, not free? I’m terribly lonely.” Commenting on this diary, Kollontai confidently offered a solution to the heroine’s torment: “Don’t we hear in this complaint a woman from the past who is used to being surrounded by familiar and beloved voices, and to feeling someone’s habitual caresses?” Kollontai’s new woman resolutely withstood such traditional longings: “She goes away, quietly smiling at him at parting, she goes to seek her dream of happiness, she goes, carrying her own soul with her, as if . . . it was necessary for her to build a new life for herself.” Solitude in this reading was less a curse than an achievement, a first step toward self-realization as a modern woman.
然而，柯伦泰的建议似乎并没有明显改变齐娜伊达·德尼谢夫斯卡娅的生活。从莫斯科女子高等课程毕业后，她回到沃罗涅日，住在父母家中，这在传统上适合未婚年轻女性。而且她继续哀叹生活中缺乏爱情。或许最重要的是，“新女性”的词汇在随后的几年里从德尼谢夫斯卡娅的日记中消失了——这是一个引人注目的发展，因为那是革命年代，新女性的理想正风靡一时。

Yet Kollontai’s advice did not appear to change Zinaida Denisevskaya’s life in appreciable ways. After graduating from the Women’s Higher Courses in Moscow, she returned to Voronezh and lived in her parents’ household, as traditionally befitted an unmarried young woman. And she continued to deplore the lack of love in her life. Most significantly perhaps, the lexicon of the new woman disappeared from Denisevskaya’s diary in subsequent years—a remarkable development given that these were the years of the revolution, when the ideal of the new woman was in full swing.

zh: 旧知识分子

children: 第一次世界大战爆发后，德尼谢夫斯卡娅“关切地”关注着“战争和俄罗斯的公共生活”，并遗憾自己无法参与她在报纸上读到的“俄罗斯社会的重生”。她对革命的爆发表示欢迎，认为这是一个高潮性事件，使“俄罗斯社会”第一次能够为了人民的利益行使政治权力。作为一名教师，她可以在全国性的公民教育运动中发挥虽然微小但重要的作用，因为她向学生们解释了“当前最广泛使用的术语的含义：宪法、君主制、共和制、最高权力等”。德尼谢夫斯卡娅反复强调她对公共事件的兴趣，并抱歉地指出，她的日记虽然仍主要处理个人的幻想和孤独，但仅反映了她兴趣和追求的一小部分。

然而，在内战日益严重的社会和政治两极分化中，德尼谢夫斯卡娅关于统一、有机俄罗斯社会的理想化观念破灭了。到1917年秋天，这一观念已从她的词汇中消失。从一个想象中的中间立场出发，她观察到了政治版图的断裂。她对苏维埃政府提出了严厉批评，认为这是一个由腐败、追逐权力且没受过教育的分子组成的政权，他们与博爱、公正的崇高社会主义理想毫无共同之处。但她对所谓的“知识分子”——社会中受过教育的成员——的批评至少同样严厉，因为他们以“怨恨、仇恨和幸灾乐祸”的态度评论布尔什维克政权的失误，并在此过程中忘记了为人民工作的职责。即使面临被“总机器的轮子”意外碾碎的危险，也不是放弃这一职责的理由，因为历史规律仍在发挥作用。当前时代是一个“过渡时期”，其标志是“人民从幼年走向青春期”。正是在谴责这一社会群体这种社会责任感缺失的“狭隘利己主义”时，德尼谢夫斯卡娅为自己争取到了一个真正知识分子的角色——在更传统和更具包容性的理解中，知识分子是教育和进步的引擎，也是未来俄罗斯民族的接生婆。即使在这个混乱和极端暴力的时代，她也在寻找一种为生活建立秩序的原则，一种从中衍生出个人世界观的意识形态。如果一种意识形态符合历史的规律性发展并服务于大众利益（在革命背景下，这只能意味着“人民”的利益），那么它就是合法的。这解释了为什么她从未站在白军一边，在精神上更接近红军，但与此同时，她也纳闷后者的残暴怎么可能表达出社会主义的“博爱与平等原则”。

After the outbreak of the First World War Denisevskaya “attentively” followed both “the war and Russia’s public life” and regretted being unable to take part in the “rebirth of Russian society” that she was reading about in the newspapers. She greeted the outbreak of revolution as a climactic event, enabling “Russian society” for the first time to exercise political power for the good of the people. As a teacher, she could claim a modest but significant role in a nationwide campaign to impart civic education to the people, as she explained to her students the “significance of the most widespread current terms: constitution, monarchy, republic, supreme power, etc.” Denisevskaya repeatedly stressed her interest in public events, and she noted apologetically that her diary, which continued to deal for the most part with personal reveries and her loneliness, reflected but a fraction of her interests and pursuits.

Yet amid the increasing social and political polarization of civil war, Denisevskaya’s idealized notion of a unified, organic Russian society evaporated. It had vanished from her vocabulary by the fall of 1917. From the vantage point of an imaginary middle, she observed the fracturing of the political landscape. She was harshly critical toward the Soviet government, a regime staffed by corrupt, power-hungry, and un-educated elements who had nothing in common with the lofty socialist ideals of brotherhood and justice. But she was at least equally critical of the “so-called intelligentsia”—educated members of society who commented with “resentment, hatred, and malicious joy” on the blunders of the Bolshevik regime and in the process lost sight of their duty to work for the people. Even the danger of being accidentally crushed by the “wheel of the general machine” was no reason to relinquish this duty, for the laws of history continued to work. The current era was a “transition period,” marked by “the people’s passing from infancy to adolescence.” It was in denouncing the socially irresponsible “narrow-minded egoism” of this social group that Denisevskaya claimed for herself the role of a true member of the intelligentsia, in its more traditional and inclusive understanding as an engine of education and progress and a midwife of the future Russian nation. Even in this time of chaos and extreme violence, she looked for a life-ordering principle,  an ideology from which to derive a personal worldview. An ideology was legitimate if it corresponded to the lawful progression of history and served a general interest, which in the context of revolution could only mean the interest of the “people.” This explains why she never sided with the White Army and was closer to the Reds in spirit, but at the same time she wondered how the latter’s brutality could possibly express the socialist “principle of brotherhood and equality.”

内战以特别严酷的方式影响了沃罗涅日。该城在冲突初期由白军控制，于1919年秋被苏维埃军队夺取。德尼谢夫斯卡娅的日记中充满了关于搜查、没收、逮捕和醉酒后的暴力行为（包括随机杀人）的描述——大部分不是第一手资料，而是基于谈话和传闻。由于被红军政府归类为有产阶级成员，德尼谢夫斯卡娅和她的父母至少经历过一次强制征税（“捐献”）。这些做法让她思考，教师作为“无产阶级知识分子”的一员，怎么可能被归入“资产阶级”之列。最终，她承认自己感到筋疲力尽、虚弱不堪，无法完全“‘接受’现实”：“在革命的压力下，面对这种随时可能发生的死亡、抢劫、惊吓以及失去亲人的风险，我慌了神。”她退缩到以城市图书馆工作为中心的生活中，“远离政治和党派问题，远离俄罗斯的公共生活……我不想在当代生活的细节中寻找方向，不想弄清谁对谁错，谁赢得了胜利，谁犯了错误。”

The civil war affected Voronezh in especially harsh ways. Held by the Whites in the early stages of the conflict, the city was seized by Soviet armies in the fall of 1919. Denisevskaya’s diary is filled with accounts—for the most part not first-hand, but based on conversations and rumors—of searches, confiscations, arrests, and drunken acts of violence, including random murder. Classified by the Red government as members of the propertied classes, Denisevskaya and her parents were at least once subjected to a forcible tax (“contribution”). Such practices left her wondering how teachers, as members of the “proletarian intelligentsia,” could be possibly grouped among the “bourgeoisie.” Ultimately, she confessed feeling too exhausted and weak to fully “‘accept’ reality”: “I lost my head under the pressure of the revolution, faced with this permanent risk of death, robbery, fright, and the loss of people dear to me.” She retreated into a life centered on her work at the city library and “far removed from politics and party questions, from the common life of Russia . . . I don’t want to find my way amid the details of contemporary life, to find out who’s right and who’s guilty, who’s achieving victories and who has made mistakes.”

与这种从世俗政治中退缩相平行的是，德尼谢夫斯卡娅越来越多地在宗教和对来世的希望中寻求逃避。她一生都虔诚信仰宗教，尽管她经常强调其信仰的现代和科学形式。对她来说，上帝作为一种“物质”、“一种特殊的能量”存在，一种像电一样的力量，当人们被爱激励并致力于善行时，这种力量就会显现，而这种神圣的能量是根据达尔文的进化规律赋予个人的。在革命的初期，德尼谢夫斯卡娅曾认为社会主义优于宗教，因为除了化身为基督教的最佳原则外，它还是一种基于科学规律的进步力量。但在面对大规模死亡和暴力时，她的基督教信仰重新抬头。受慢性心脏病和严重的黄热病折磨，德尼谢夫斯卡娅并没指望能在这些末日般的时代幸存下来。

Paralleling this retreat from secular politics, Denisevskaya increasingly sought escape in religion and the hope of an afterlife. She had been religious all her life, though she often stressed the modern and scientific form of her belief. God to her existed as a “substance,” “a special kind of energy,” a force like electricity that showed when people were animated by love and committed good deeds, and this godly energy was imparted to individuals by Darwinist laws of evolution. In the initial stages of the revolution Denisevskaya had seen socialism as superior to religion because in addition to incarnating the best principles of Christianity it was a progressive force based on scientific laws. But in the face of mass death and violence, her Christian belief rebounded. Suffering from chronic heart disease and an acute case of yellow fever, Denisevskaya did not expect to survive these apocalyptic times.

然而，她从内战中走出来时变得更加坚强，并有了新的方向感。1920年，她辞去了城市图书馆的职务，离开了父母家，到城外的一个试验站担任研究员。用她自己的话说，她从“抽象观念”的“精神”世界转向了亲自动手的、科学的、“事实的”工作。从直接意义上讲，与来自该地区和莫斯科访问农场的农学家们的合作有望让她摆脱孤独。但她的搬迁也是一种尝试，旨在摆脱被激进社会主义者丑化了的传统知识分子的那种精神和书本世界，转而拥护一种与劳动人民在一起并为之服务的应用劳动原则。她这一时期的著作表达了对过去社会和道德理想日益批判的观点，以至于她将知识分子的精神——她曾将其视为为人民服务——等同于资产阶级个人主义。然而，她在日记中对过去追随对象的否定与她为人民工作的描述并存，后者唤起了一种传统的知识分子特质。在描述在令人震惊的“落后”条件下开展农学研究的困难时，德尼谢夫斯卡娅将自己塑造为教育和道德的灯塔，是误入歧途的共产党人和愚昧人民的引导力量。她对文化和教学卓越地位的主张，与她那主张退位和服从于劳动人民的纲领性精神形成了鲜明对比。
在从事新职业几年后，德尼谢夫斯卡娅最初的热情消失了。早些时候在她看来像是一个“幸福之岛”的试验场，结果却成了无尽“沼泽”中一个孤立的文化点。当该地区农学站的新负责人帕维尔·皮斯托夫访问农场时，她深刻体会到了这一点：

对于这个身材敦实、矮个、蓝眼睛的男人，我产生了一种奇怪而令人不快的嫉妒感。他在中国和日本生活了很长时间，见多识广，博学多识。他的词汇中点缀着外来词。他是一个有文化的欧洲人，或者更准确地说，不是欧洲人而是国际主义者。我感觉到他是一个处于最高文化水平的人，非常嫉妒他……他是俄罗斯人，但我对他来说就像杜尼娅或马里沙（农民助手）对我来说一样陌生。他穿着体面的衣服，而我穿着毡靴和过时的衬衫走来走去。他见过并了解这个世界，他谈论在世界各地进行的科学工作，仿佛这些事情与他息息相关；而我什么都不知道，我从早坐到晚，做着机械的工作，我变老了，放任自流，变得不合群。

Yet she came out of the civil war stronger, and with a new sense of direction. In 1920 she relinquished her position at the city library and left her parents’ home, to take up work as a researcher at an experimental station outside of the city. In her own words, she transferred from a “mental” world of “abstract ideas” to hands-on, scientific, “factual” work. In an immediate sense, collaboration with the agronomists from the region and from Moscow who visited the farm promised escape from her loneliness. But her move was also an attempt to shed the mental and bookish domain of the traditional intelligentsia, as it was caricaturized by the radical socialists, and to embrace a principle of applied labor with and for the toiling people. Her writings of this period expressed an increasingly critical view of the social and moral ideals of her past, to the point that she equated the spirit of the intelligentsia— which she had once seen as service to the people—with bourgeois individualism. Yet her repudiations of past allegiances coexisted in the diary with descriptions of her work for the people which evoked a traditional intelligentsia ethos. In describing the difficulties of conducting agronomical research in conditions of appalling “backwardness,” Denisevskaya cast herself as a beacon of education and morality, a guiding force for both erring Communists and the benighted people. Her claim to cultural and pedagogical preeminence stood in marked contrast to her programmatic spirit of abdication and subservience to the laboring people.

Several years into her new profession, Denisevskaya’s initial enthusiasm was gone. The experimental farm, which had earlier appeared to her as a “happy island,” turned out to be an isolated spot of culture in the midst of an interminable “swamp.” This was brought home to her when the new director of the region’s agronomical stations, Pavel Pistsov, visited the farm:

I experienced a strange and unpleasant feeling of envy for this stocky, short, blue-eyed man. He lived in China and Japan for a long time, he has seen, knows, and understands much. His vocabulary is peppered with foreign words. He is a cultured European, or more exactly, not a European but an internationalist. I sensed him to be a person at the highest level of culture and envied him strongly . . . He is Russian, but I am as strange to him as Dunya or Marisha [peasant assistants] is to me. He wears cultured clothes, while I walk around in felt boots and an old-fashioned blouse. He has seen and knows the world, he talks about scientific work conducted all over the world, as if these were things that were close to him; and I don’t know anything, I sit from morning till night, doing mechanical work, I’ve grown old, let myself go, become unsociable.
皮斯托夫似乎符合德尼谢夫斯卡娅对知识分子的理想化观念：受过高等教育，穿着和言谈优雅，从事具有普世范围的前沿科学工作。这些特征突显了她自己在物质和文化上的匮乏。或许最引人注目的是，她觉得与这位站长相比，自己显得苍老且消瘦，尽管她只有39岁——正好是皮斯托夫的年纪。

20世纪20年代后期是德尼谢夫斯卡娅的个人危机时期，这戏剧性地打破了她早期日记中那种消极退守的基调。她描述了一种真正的自我丧失，这是由于她的信念崩塌和个人使命感的缺失造成的。她觉得自己正在漂流，无法控制病弱的身体和神经：“一切都是那么不稳定、混乱、出人意料。从各个方向，不幸、疾病、痛苦和死亡降临到你身上……我失去了我的哲学，我失去了对神经的控制，我就像海带，在浪花中摇摆。”在物质上，她享受着基本的舒适（“我有一个温暖的房间，一张软床，我可以生活、吃喝和工作”），但在精神上，她感到彻底空虚。她缺失的“主要东西”是爱。“这就是我没什么可写的原因……总是同一个故事：孤独，变幻莫测的情绪。一会儿高涨——一会儿低落，一会儿再次高涨，一会儿又低落……而且总是低谷比高峰更深、持续时间更长。”

Pistsov seemed to fit Denisevskaya’s idealized notion of the intelligentsia: highly educated, refined in dress and speech, engaged in cutting-edge scientific work with a universal scope. These features underscored her own material and cultural destitution. Most striking perhaps was that she saw herself appearing old and wasted compared with the director, though she was only 39 years old—exactly Pistsov’s age.

The latter half of the 1920s was a time of personal crisis for Denisevskaya, dramatically punctuating the quietist tone of her earlier diary. She described a veritable loss of self, brought about by her crushed convictions and lack of a personal mission. She felt she was drifting, in-capable of directing her sick body and nerves: “Everything is so unstable, confused, unexpected. From all directions misfortunes, illnesses, suffering, and death come down on you . . . I have lost my philosophy, I have lost control of my nerves, I’ve become like seaweed, swaying in the surf.” Materially she enjoyed basic comforts (“I have a warm room, a soft bed, I can live, eat, drink, and work”), but spiritually she felt utterly void. The “main thing” she lacked was love. “That is why I have nothing to write about . . . Always one and the same story: loneliness, shifting moods. Up—and down, up again, and down again . . . And invariably the downfalls are deeper and last longer than my peaks.”

德尼谢夫斯卡娅在日记中从个人角度提出的关于生活和社会使命的问题，也是苏维埃权力中心辩论的主题。争论的焦点是“资产阶级专家”，即像德尼谢夫斯卡娅这样在革命前受过教育和熏陶的专业人士，他们现在向政权提供专业知识，但不接受共产主义事业。共产主义活动家不屑地将这种“旧的”、“资产阶级的”专家与一种“新的”、尚未形成的苏维埃知识分子相对比，后者应全身心地致力于政治体制。反过来，这个处于困境中的群体的成员寻求保留一定程度的政治独立性，同时强调他们对苏维埃秩序的基本忠诚。在1925年莫斯科的一次公开辩论中，一位学者捍卫了知识分子的文化资历，这些资历集中体现在“英雄式的乡村女教师”身上。这位知识分子的灯塔，在远离文明前哨的落后村庄，应对政治逆境、微薄的收入和悲惨的生活条件，以极大的精力“创造”了她“平凡而伟大的事业”。

The questions about her life and social mission that Denisevskaya posed in personal terms in her diary were also subjects of debate at the very center of Soviet power. At issue were the “bourgeois specialists,” professionals like Denisevskaya, who had been educated and formed before the revolution and now lent the regime their expertise without embracing the Communist cause. Communist activists disdainfully contrasted this “old,” “bourgeois” specialist to a “new,” yet to be formed, Soviet intelligentsia, which was to be devoted to the political regime body and soul. In turn, members of the embattled group sought to retain a degree of political independence while stressing their basic loyalty to the Soviet order. At a public debate in Moscow in 1925, a scholar defended the intelligentsia’s cultural credentials, which were epitomized in the “heroic type of the female village teacher.” Coping with political adversity, a meager income, and miserable living conditions in a backward village, far from the outposts of civilization, this beacon of the intelligentsia “created” with the utmost energy her “modest, yet great deed.”

这种对政治自治的恳求遭到了布尔什维克党首席理论家尼古拉·布哈林的激烈驳斥。布哈林坚持认为，政治和文化不能被视为独立的活动领域：“你以这种方式建造大厦，使文化层面看起来独立于政治层面。但这种东西是不存在的。”根据布哈林的说法，知识分子在对待革命行动的态度上因其传统的懦弱而进一步受阻。这一特征根植于根深蒂固的个人主义，这种个人主义阻止了资产阶级专家阶级欣赏工人阶级的集体力量和历史伟力。布哈林抨击了知识分子对苏维埃权力政策在道德上的保留意见，他将其定性为害怕弄脏双手。在目前激烈的阶级斗争形势下，如果不求助于暴力，革命政治就无法进行。在这种条件下，那些自称害怕“踏过尸体”的人实际上是潜伏的反动分子。然而，布哈林提出的核心指控是，尽管知识分子宣称信奉民粹主义，但他们并没有真正致力于解放人民，不愿放弃他们对启蒙的垄断。他们更喜欢代表人民讲道和发言，而不是让人民自己说话。最后，布哈林邀请知识分子加入共产主义政权，以实现其“巨大的普遍标准”，并培养一种新的苏维埃知识分子：“我们将大批量产出受过教育的个人，就像在工厂里制造他们一样……如果我们设定了走向共产主义的任务，我们就必须让所有事情都充满这项任务。”
在接下来的几年里，德尼谢夫斯卡娅几乎按字面把布哈林勾勒的方案变成了自己的行动，令人惊讶。她转而反对她内心和她社交环境中的“旧知识分子”，面对被归咎于她的懦弱，并在对待政治和建设社会主义社会方面采取了更具“党性”的立场。这是一个惊人的转变。它是如何发生的？

This plea for political autonomy met with a fierce rebuttal from the Bolshevik party’s chief ideologist, Nikolai Bukharin. Politics and culture could not be viewed as separate fields of action, Bukharin insisted: “You build the edifice in such a way that the cultural row appears to be independent from the political one. But such a thing doesn’t exist.” The intelligentsia was further crippled in its stance toward revolutionary action, according to Bukharin, by its traditional faintheartedness. This trait was rooted in an ingrained individualism which prevented the class of bourgeois specialists from appreciating the collective power and historic might of the working class. Bukharin attacked the intelligentsia’s ethical reservations about the policies of Soviet power, which he characterized as its fear of dirtying its hands. In the present situation of intense class struggle, revolutionary politics could not be carried out without recourse to violence. Under these conditions those who professed a fear of “stepping over corpses” were in fact covert reactionaries. The central charge brought by Bukharin, however, was that, in spite of its professed populism, the intelligentsia was not really committed to emancipating the people, being reluctant to give up its monopoly on enlightenment. It preferred to preach and speak on the people’s behalf rather than letting them speak for themselves. In concluding, Bukharin invited the intelligentsia to join the Communist regime in realizing its “gigantic universal standards” and in rearing a new, Soviet intelligentsia: “We will produce educated individuals in great numbers, we will manufacture them just like in a factory . . . If we set ourselves the task of going toward Communism we have to infuse everything with this task.”

In strikingly literal fashion, in the following years, Denisevskaya appropriated for herself the scenario outlined by Bukharin. She turned against the “old intelligentsia”—both inside her and in her social environment—confronted the faintheartedness ascribed to her, and assumed a more “party-minded” stance toward politics and the building of a socialist society. This was a stunning turnaround. How did it come about?

苏维埃政权针对“旧的”、“资产阶级”知识分子发动的无情宣传，无疑在构建德尼谢夫斯卡娅的选择和偏好方面发挥了重要作用。这种主要表现为言语暴力的行为在20世纪20年代末得到了扩大和系统化，最终演变为残酷的骚扰、逮捕、做秀式审判和处决——其中一些就发生在德尼谢夫斯卡娅的附近。这种大规模暴力直到1930年才出现在德尼谢夫斯卡娅的日记中，这远在她开始转向苏维埃事业之后。决定性的一点是，布哈林所概述的苏维埃愿景对德尼谢夫斯卡娅极具吸引力。她终生的几项承诺——追求连贯的世界观、与历史规律一致的有意义的人生使命，以及创造完美的人格和社会——现在都由国家带给了她。除了智识上的实质内容，这些思想因其整合潜力而诱人。正是为了融入集体，她才疏远了她定义的个人主义、自私、边缘和消极的“旧知识分子”，转而拥护苏维埃政权宣传的普遍主义。德尼谢夫斯卡娅在社会主义主体性的殿堂中为自己建立了一个新家。社会主义主体性对不同的个人有着不同的含义；对她来说，它提供了一种庞大的、公共的生活，充满了温暖、爱和归属感，减轻了她的个人孤独。

The relentless propaganda generated by the Soviet regime against the “old,” “bourgeois” intelligentsia undoubtedly played an important role in structuring Denisevskaya’s choices and preferences. This largely verbal violence was broadened and systematized toward the end of the 1920s, culminating in brutal harassment, arrests, show trials, and executions—some of them in Denisevskaya’s immediate vicinity. This massive violence appears in Denisevskaya’s diary only in 1930, well after the onset of her conversion to the Soviet cause. The decisive point is that the Soviet vision as outlined by Bukharin was immensely appealing to Denisevskaya. Several of her lifelong commitments—the quest for a co-herent worldview, a meaningful mission in life consonant with the laws of history, and the creation of a perfect human personality and society—were now brought to her by the state. Beyond their intellectual substance, these ideas were tantalizing for their integrative potential. It was for the sake of integration into the collective that she distanced herself from the “old intelligentsia,” which she defined as individualist, selfish, marginal, and negative, and embraced the universalism propagated by the Soviet regime. Denisevskaya built a new home for herself in an edifice of socialist subjectivity. Socialist subjectivity had differing meanings for different individuals; for her it afforded a large, communal life, filled with warmth, love, and a sense of belonging that mitigated her personal loneliness.

zh: 阿廖沙

children: 这些新思想的力量可以通过德尼谢夫斯卡娅在20世纪20年代中期到30年代初期对身边几个人的性格描述的变化来衡量。其中有费迪南多夫一家：瓦西里·弗拉基米罗维奇（日记中的“V.V.”），她在试验农场的上级，以及他的妻子尤利安娜·瓦西里耶夫娜（“J.V.”）。德尼谢夫斯卡娅和这对夫妇住在同一栋楼里——很有可能是在同一个公用公寓里——她把他们的家描述为荒凉草原上的文化前哨。1926年底，当费迪南多夫一家搬到沃罗涅日市（V.V.受聘于新成立的兽医学院）时，德尼谢夫斯卡娅恐惧地想到她很快就会失去“成千上万的便利和乐趣”，包括J.V.的钢琴独奏和珍贵的关于文化和政治主题的晚间讨论。她评论说，V.V.的新任命是苏维埃政权如何“彻底混乱”的又一个迹象。课程在一周内就要开始了，尽管学院仅存在于纸面上，缺乏校舍、教学人员和资金。她总结道：“现在生活在俄罗斯太无聊、太令人厌恶了！”很可能她的话回响了V.V.自己的愤慨，从而传达了她与费迪南多夫一家谈话的感觉。

然而，仅仅几个月后，当德尼谢夫斯卡娅在城里拜访这对夫妇时（正如她指出的那样，是在“旧圣诞节”假期），她的描述中带有一丝疏离感，这种隔阂在接下来的几个月和几年里还会扩大：“J.V.像是一本时尚杂志上的照片。V.V.显得很有城市感，也很遥远。”从现在起，她对费迪南多夫一家的访问之后，都会对他们的“知识分子”圈子发表批评。她对知识分子评论彼此以及社会和政治发展时表现出的那种没完没了的讽刺和争吵感到不满。与此同时，她似乎害怕表达自己的观点：
我对保持沉默、不直言不讳，以及我的思想与周围人思想之间的差异感到厌倦。我惊讶于这些人中大多数人那种狭隘的个人生活观。如果没有白面包或白布，就意味着生活不好。但其他人的生活在许多方面已经变得更好这一事实却不被考虑。他们对一切都幸灾乐祸，对一切都冷嘲热讽。人会对这种对一切持续不断的敌意感到厌烦。
随着德尼谢夫斯卡娅将费迪南多夫一家重塑为旧时代的和过时的代表，她对年轻一代共产党人和专家表现出了更大的同情，她认为这些人是苏维埃秩序的支柱。这种视角的转变是由她的新职业职责促成的：1928年，她在V.V.工作的同一所兽医学院的家禽养殖系担任教职。她没有放弃在试验农场的工作，但更频繁地往返于城市和学院之间。正是在那里，她对年轻人的热情（最初并非没有保留）占据了上风。

The strength of these new ideas can be gauged by Denisevskaya’s evolving characterization of several people close to her between the mid-1920s and the early 1930s. There were the Ferdinandovs, Vasily Vladimirovich (“V.V.” in the diary), her supervisor on the experimental farm, and his wife, Juliana Vasilevna (“J.V.”). Denisevskaya lived in the same building as the couple—quite possibly in the same communal apartment—and she described their household as an outpost of culture in the forbidding steppe. When, in late 1926, the Ferdinandovs moved to the city of Voronezh, where V.V. had been appointed to a newly established veterinary institute, Denisevskaya thought with horror about the “thousands of conveniences and pleasures” she would soon lose, including J.V.’s piano recitals and cherished evening discussions on cultural and political themes. V.V.’s new appointment, she remarked, was another indication of how “completely muddled” Soviet power was. Courses were to begin within a week, even though the institute existed only on paper and lacked a building, teaching staff, and money. “It is so dull and repelling to live in Russia right now!” she concluded. It is likely that her words echoed V.V.’s own indignation, and thus convey a sense of her conversations with the Ferdinandovs.

However, only a few months later, when Denisevskaya visited the couple in the city (for the “Old Christmas” holiday, as she pointed out), there was a note of estrangement in her description, a gap that was to widen in the months and years to come: “J.V. is like a picture from a fashion journal. V.V. appears urban and distant.” From now on, her visits to the Ferdinandovs would be followed by critical remarks on their “intelligentsia” milieu. She took exception to the permanent sarcasm and bickering with which members of the intelligentsia commented on one another as well as on social and political developments. At the same time she seemed to be afraid to articulate her own views:

I’m getting tired of keeping silent, of not speaking out, and of the discrepancy between my thoughts and the thoughts of the people around me. I am amazed by the narrow personal outlook on life that most of these people have. If there is no white bread or no white cloth, it means life is bad. But the fact that other people’s lives have become better in many respects is not taken into account. And they gloat over everything, speak ironically about everything. One becomes bored with this constant hostility toward everything.

As Denisevskaya recast the Ferdinandovs as representatives of an old and outlived world, she showed greater sympathy to a young generation of Communists and specialists whom she saw as the mainstays of the Soviet order. This change in perspective was spurred by her new professional duties: in 1928 she took up a teaching position in the poultry farming division of the same veterinary institute at which V.V. worked. She did not give up her work on the experimental farm, but commuted more frequently to the city and the institute. It was there that her enthusiasm for the young people, initially not without reservations, overtook her.

当她遇到她的新同事时，她自发地将他们分为“旧”和“新”两代，宣称自己被新的一代所吸引：“我的心飞向了新的一代。”她立刻喜欢上了分配给她的一名实习生安东尼娜·塔塔尔斯基赫，她拥有坚强的意志、务实的导向，以及不可动摇的乐观和开朗。日记中用来描述另一位年轻同事——29岁的列宁格勒专家伊万·谢尔盖耶维奇·斯梅奇尼科夫（当时正访问沃罗涅日）的特征几乎完全相同。德尼谢夫斯卡娅“认真仔细地”观察这些人，从他们身上认出了新兴的共产主义新人的原型。她在谈到斯梅奇尼科夫时评论说：“一种新的类型，充满活力”；她将塔塔尔斯基赫描述为“某种新女性”，具有“新的、人类女性的本质”。这两人分别来自遥远的省份——坦波夫地区和“彼尔姆森林深处”，这些新人无法表现出像J.V.及其圈子那样的文化修养，但由于他们积极参与社会和政治生活并致力于建设未来，这些新人远比他们优越：“他们是我在俄罗斯知识分子身上所重视和爱戴的东西的继承者。”

As she encountered her new colleagues, she spontaneously divided them into “old” and “new” generations, proclaiming her attraction to the new: “My heart flew to the new.” She immediately took a liking to an intern assigned to her, Antonina Tatarskikh, who possessed strength of mind, a practical orientation, and an unshakable optimism and cheer. Virtually the same features appeared in the diary to characterize another young colleague, Ivan Sergeevich Smychnikov, a 29-year-old specialist from Leningrad on a visit to Voronezh. Denisevskaya studied these people “attentively and carefully,” recognizing in them prototypes of the emerging Communist new man. “A new type, vital,” she remarked on Smychnikov, and Tatarskikh she described as “some sort of a new woman,” with a “new, human-female essence.” Both hailing from distant provinces, the Tambov region and “the depths of the Perm forests” respectively, these new people could not display the same cultured manners as J.V. and her circle, but were in-finitely superior to them because of their active participation in social and political life and their commitment to building the future: “They are the heirs to what I valued and loved about the Russian intelligentsia.”

在对这些年轻人和新人的反思中，齐娜伊达·德尼谢夫斯卡娅爱上了其中一个。他的名字叫阿列克谢·斯捷潘诺维奇·丹科夫；她叫他阿廖沙。两人相识多年，但直到她对年轻一代产生浪漫向往后，德尼谢夫斯卡娅才认真地与他交往。由于她写给他并抄录在笔记本上的一系列信件，他们的关系得到了很好的记录。他们这段于1932年结束的关系史，使我们能够追踪德尼谢夫斯卡娅如何逐渐重新定义对自己和伴侣的看法，并将他塑造成新一代的象征。德尼谢夫斯卡娅对这段关系的描述极具个人色彩，充满了情感和欲望，但它也可以被解读为对旧的资产阶级知识分子与新的苏维埃知识分子之间社会和政治关系的探究。个人之爱和意识形态取向的语义在德尼谢夫斯卡娅那里是如此交织，以至于她和阿廖沙是否能真正相互理解并成为一对爱侣的问题，同时也是她作为旧秩序的代表是否能在新苏维埃制度中找到永久归宿的问题。

In the midst of these reflections on the young and new people, Zinaida Denisevskaya fell in love with one of them. His name was Alexei Stepanovich Dankov; she called him Alyosha. The two had known each other for several years, but only after developing her romance with the young generation did Denisevskaya become seriously involved with him. Their relationship is well documented, thanks especially to a series of letters she sent to him and copied into a notebook. The history of their relationship, which ended in 1932, allows us to trace Denisevskaya’s gradual redefinition of her view of herself and of her partner, whom she remade into an icon of the new generation. Denisevskaya’s description of this relationship was highly personal, brimming with feelings and desires, but it can also be read as an inquiry into the social and political relationship between the old, bourgeois intelligentsia and the new, Soviet one. The semantics of personal love and ideological orientation were so intertwined for Denisevskaya that the question of whether she and Alyosha could truly understand each other and become a loving couple was at the same time a question of whether she as a representative of the old order could find a permanent home in the new Soviet system.
阿廖沙比德尼谢夫斯卡娅小十六岁；他们似乎从20世纪20年代初就认识了，当时他作为一名学徒加入试验农场。那时他大约20岁，而她三十五岁上下。

1925年他离开农场去莫斯科学习。他们早期关系的细节尚不清楚，但他从莫斯科写信给她说，他仍然爱她，她对他来说意味着一切。为了证明这一点，他补充道——用当时共产主义的爱情语言——他无法停止手淫。德尼谢夫斯卡娅觉得他很可怜。正如她在日记中所记，他误解了她温柔的、母亲般的爱意并产生了性冲动：“他无法控制自己的本能，让自己被它奴役。”她对他持有一种居高临下的态度。她报告说曾试图启蒙他，让他明白简单的生理欲望与复杂的爱情心理之间的区别，但最终放弃了：“当我试图让他了解他自己时，他什么都不懂。”她对一位朋友吐露说阿廖沙让她感到无聊：他从莫斯科来访，但由于一直在学习，说不出关于首都的有趣事情。

Alyosha was sixteen years younger than Denisevskaya; they seem to have known each other from the early 1920s when he joined the experimental farm as an apprentice. He was then about 20 and she in her mid-30s.

He left the farm in 1925 to study in Moscow. Details of their early relationship are unknown, but he wrote to her from Moscow that he still loved her and that she meant everything to him. To prove this, he added—in the contemporary Communist language of love—that he could not stop masturbating. Denisevskaya felt sorry for him. As she noted in the diary, he had misinterpreted her tender, motherly affection and become aroused: “He was unable to master his instinct and let himself be enslaved by it.” Her attitude toward him was patronizing. She reported trying to enlighten him about the difference between simple physiological urges and the complex psychology of love, but ultimately gave up: “He doesn’t understand anything, when I try to make him understand himself.” To a friend she confided that Alyosha bored her: he had come from Moscow for a visit, but had nothing interesting to say about the capital, because he had been studying all the time.

阿廖沙随后从日记中消失了三年，直到1929年9月，他到沃罗涅日访问两周，并向德尼谢夫斯卡娅求婚。她拒绝了他。在一条富有启发性的日记条目中，她解释道：“啊，如果我能改变一点点，改变他举止和性格中一些微小的特征……也许我内心的疏离感就会消失，[这种感觉]阻止了我内心产生相互的柔情。他告别时点头的方式，他笨拙的身影，他说话的方式……我想为他和为我痛哭。”她完全通过有教养的知识分子的镜头来评价阿廖沙，对他不够文雅的举止感到尴尬：“当我们单独在一起时，在他温柔、有力的怀抱里感觉很好，但看到他笨拙、尴尬，缺乏任何文化技能，这让我很不愉快，这让尤利安娜·瓦西里耶夫娜不自觉地想要保护他。”在意识层面上，她不再想尊重旧知识分子的意见，但她忍不住像J.V.那样对待阿廖沙，她因此讨厌她的老朋友，也讨厌她自己。

与阿廖沙在一起激发出她内心乡村教师的一面。当他在返回莫斯科后她写信给他时，她以一种居高临下的态度对他说话，像对待一个愿意学习但智力有限的学生，混合了鼓励和责备。她解释说，他们达成相互理解是“绝对不可能”的，因为他们是“不同世界、不同世代的人。我们最后一次相遇彻底颠覆了我内心的某些东西。有时我想哭，因为你不是我希望看到的样子。”她承认他的个性多年来有所成长，并称赞他的感情“真诚”且“纯洁”，但她想知道他的“心理”是否也得到了相应的发展，变得“更精致”和“深刻”。这封信自始至终充满了教导意味，以劝诫结束：“请至少在你生命中写一次理性的、详细的、真诚的信。只有这将决定我们未来的关系将采取何种形式。不要急，花几天时间写信会更好。祝一切顺利！”她还评论说，虽然她直觉上用非正式的“你”（ty）称呼他，但他应该始终正式且尊敬地称呼她，因为“‘您’（Vy）对你来说比‘你’意味着更多。你对每个人都用‘你’。”在留存下来的唯一一封他的回信中，他确实称呼她为“齐娜伊达·安东诺夫娜”。相比之下，她总是叫他“阿廖沙”。

Alyosha then disappeared from the diary for three years, until September 1929, when he visited Voronezh for two weeks—and proposed to Denisevskaya. She turned him down. In a revealing diary entry she explained: “Ah, if I could only alter just a bit, some minor traits in his manner and character . . . perhaps the feeling of alienation inside me would die away, [a feeling] which prevents a reciprocal tenderness from swelling up inside me. The way he nods when saying farewell, his clumsy figure, his manner of speaking . . . I want to cry from pain for him and for me.” She evaluated Alyosha entirely through the lens of the cultured intelligentsia, feeling embarrassed by his unrefined behavior: “It feels good to be in his tender, strong arms when we are alone, but it is unpleasant to see him clumsy and awkward, lacking any cultural skills, which unintentionally makes Juliana Vasilevna want to protect him.” On a conscious level she no longer wanted to respect the opinions of the old intelligentsia, but she could not help relating to Alyosha as J.V. did, and she hated her old friend for that, and herself as well.

Being with Alyosha brought out the village schoolteacher in her. When she wrote to him after his return to Moscow, she addressed him condescendingly, as a willing but intellectually limited student, with a mix of encouragement and reproach. It was “absolutely impossible” for them, she explained, to reach a mutual understanding, for they were “people of different worlds, of different generations. Our last encounter turned something upside-down inside me. Sometimes I want to cry because you are not as I would like to see you.” She acknowledged that his personality had grown over the years, and she commended him for the “sincerity” and “purity” of his feelings, but she wondered whether his “psyche” had developed commensurably, and become “more re-fined” and “profound.” The letter, didactic throughout, ended with exhortations: “At least once in your life, write, please, a sensible, detailed, sincere letter. Only this will decide which form our relations will assume in the future. Don’t rush, it would be better to write the letter over several days. All the best!” She also remarked that while she intuitively addressed him with the informal “thou” (ty) he should always address her formally and respectfully, because “‘You’ (Vy) means more to you than ‘thou.’ You address everybody with ‘thou’.” In the only surviving letter from him he indeed addressed her as “Zinaida Antonovna.” By contrast, she invariably called him “Alyosha.”

也许是出乎意料，这段关系确实有了进展。10月下旬，在阿廖沙再次来访前几天，她在日记中记下，她同意嫁给他，尽管只是“非正式地”、在身体关系上，这意味着不是出自真心。在这次访问中，当她意识到他在共产党内的投入、他的政治和社会发展时，她开始以新的眼光看待他。德尼谢夫斯卡娅忍不住审视她的年轻丈夫；他是那些她“像读新书一样……专注且专心地”研读的新人之一。齐娜伊达以前不予考虑或忽视的阿廖沙的个人特质，如V.V.赞扬他“有活力”且“积极”，或她自己承认的真诚、纯洁和力量，开始以新的方式产生共鸣，将他重塑为典型的新人。这是对一个直到不久前还被她嘲笑为没有教养的笨拙男孩的人的全面重新评估。

Unexpectedly, perhaps, the relationship did progress. In late October, a few days before Alyosha was to visit again, she noted in the diary that she had agreed to marry him, though only “unofficially” and physically, meaning not with her heart. During this visit she came to see him in a new light, as she recognized his investment in the Communist party, his political and social development. Denisevskaya couldn’t help scrutinizing her young husband; he was one of the new people whom she read “like new books . . . attentively and intently.” Personal characteristics of Alyosha that Zinaida had previously dismissed or ignored, like V.V.’s praise that he was “vital” and “active” or her own acknowledgment of his sincerity, purity, and strength, began to resonate in new ways, recasting him into a model new man. This was a sweeping reconsideration of a person whom until shortly before she had ridiculed as an awkward boy with no manners.

对政治的新立场定义了德尼谢夫斯卡娅对阿廖沙的重新评价。政治意识取代文化成为“个人发展”的衡量标准，在这一领域，阿廖沙比她成熟“一百倍”。德尼谢夫斯卡娅现在宣布她与政治领域（特别是党派政治）有了新的亲近感，而她以前一直厌恶政治，认为其自私、暴力且不公正：“即使是阶级政治——作为孤独的知识分子的我最不能理解的东西——也开始对我产生意义了。”她写道，随着她与阿廖沙关系的加深，她的政治观点也在发生变化：“俄罗斯的公共生活对我来说变得更加亲切，其中的一切都变得更加可以理解了。”德尼谢夫斯卡娅在这一背景下反复使用的“理解”一词颇具启发性：这位长期试图教导阿廖沙文化和儒雅举止的前教师，现在把他视为某种政治老师。她的看法与当时党的领导人对无产阶级相对于知识分子地位的描述非常接近。无产阶级要扮演“教育阶级”的角色，使那些不反对苏维埃计划的资产阶级专家充满意识形态上的坚定和意志力。

A new stance toward politics defined Denisevskaya’s reappraisal of Alyosha. Political consciousness replaced culture as the yardstick of “personal development,” and in this domain Alyosha was “a hundred times” more mature than she was. Denisevskaya now proclaimed a new closeness with the political sphere, and specifically with party politics, which she had formerly abhorred as egotistical, violent, and unjust: “Even class politics—the thing that I as a member of the solitary intelligentsia could understand least—is beginning to make sense to me.” Along with her deepening intimacy with Alyosha, she wrote, she was undergoing a change in her political views: “The common life of Russia has become more dear to me, everything in [Russia] has become more understandable.” The term “understand,” which Denisevskaya used repeatedly in this context, was revealing: this former teacher, who had long sought to teach Alyosha lessons of culture and polished manners, now considered him a political teacher of sorts. Her view was very close to the way party leaders at the time represented the proletariat vis-à-vis the intelligentsia. The proletariat was to act as an “educating class,” imbuing those bourgeois specialists who did not oppose the Soviet project with ideological steadfastness and willpower.

总的来说，德尼谢夫斯卡娅记录的取向变化遵循了布哈林为知识分子规定的步骤：它必须放弃其文化特权，打破其种姓般的孤立，在布尔什维克党的坚定引导下前进。她通过嫁给一个年轻的共产党人，以字面方式执行了这一计划。但值得注意的是，德尼谢夫斯卡娅对阿廖沙和她自己的新描述是对她先前评估的阐发而非否定，因此具有显著的有机特征。她不是一个在压力下屈服并放弃先前观点的“老知识分子”。相反，她正在进行的重新定义在吸收新特征的同时，保留了许多传统特征。和以前一样，阿廖沙是她的教育对象（一个“男孩”，一个“儿子”），但此外他日益呈现为一个人格成熟的“人”、一个意识形态伙伴（“兄弟”）和潜在的心理灵魂伴侣（“丈夫”）。

嫁给阿廖沙后，德尼谢夫斯卡娅遭遇了一系列的冲突、斗争和误解。以民族志的热情研究新的共产主义一代是一回事，而与一个忠诚的共产党人建立关系则是另一回事。在婚后写给他的第一封信中，她想知道他们怎么可能“结合、统一和调和”他们截然相反的期望。因为她年龄较大，她在“爱情方面比你更苛求。我想要比我们两人目前经历的更复杂的情感、更深刻的快乐、更多的相互滋养……而你希望我拥有更好的健康，对你的兴趣有更好的理解，具备辩论的能力并表现出更大的政治和公共发展……难道不是这样吗？”德尼谢夫斯卡娅坚持寻求培养爱情的心理维度。阿廖沙几乎一直不在她身边，所以她在写给他的信中阐述了她对他们共同未来的看法。阿廖沙很少回复，即使回复，也仅限于简短的便条：
1929年12月17日：昨天我收到了阿廖沙的一张明信片。又是那套老话：他忙得不可开交，没时间写，也不知道怎么写；他在某些事情上同意我，而在另一些事情上不同意。他觉得我的很多问题很奇怪。对他来说，似乎一切都很清楚，一切都是不言而喻的。而且……没有一个温暖的字眼，甚至没有一丝爱意的暗示……他不懂得如何去爱。

Overall, the change in orientation that Denisevskaya documented followed the steps Bukharin had stipulated for the intelligentsia: it had to abdicate its cultural prerogative, break out of its caste-like isolation, and proceed under the firm, guiding hand of the Bolshevik party. She enacted this program in literal fashion by marrying a young Communist. But it is noteworthy, too, that Denisevskaya’s new description of Alyosha and herself elaborated rather than repudiated her previous assessment, and had thus a remarkably organic character. She was not an “old intelligent” who capitulated under pressure and renounced her previous views. Instead her ongoing redefinition retained a number of traditional features while incorporating new traits. As before, Alyosha was an object of her education (a “boy,” a “son”), but in addition he emerged increasingly as a developed personality (“human being”), an ideological partner (“brother”) and a potential psychological soul mate (“husband”).

In marrying Alyosha, Denisevskaya ran into a series of conflicts, struggles, and misunderstandings. It was one thing to study the new Communist generation with ethnographic passion, and another to engage in a relationship with a dedicated Communist. In one of her first letters to him after their wedding, she wondered how they could possibly “combine, agree on, and reconcile” their contrary expectations. Because she was older, she was more “demanding in love than you are. I want more complex feelings, more profound joys, more mutual nurturing than the two of us are experiencing . . . While you want from me better health, better understanding of your interests, the ability to argue and demonstrate greater political and public development . . . Isn’t this true?” Denisevskaya persistently sought to cultivate a psychological dimension of love. Alyosha was away from her nearly all the time, so she formulated her views on their common future in letters to him. Alyosha rarely answered, and when he did, he limited himself to brief notes:

12/17/1929 Yesterday I received a postcard from Alyosha. Once again the usual thing: he is terribly busy, he has no time to write and doesn’t know how; he agrees with me about some things, while disagreeing about others. He finds many of my questions strange. To him it seems that everything is clear, that everything goes without saying. And . . . not a single warm word, not even a hint of affection . . . He doesn’t know how to love.

她满怀期待地盼望着他在1930年2月的下一次沃罗涅日之访。阿廖沙只呆了两天，但这足以粉碎她的期待。正如她向日记吐露的那样，她曾想第一次看到他完全赤裸的样子，以便直接、全然地体验他对她的情感，但相反，这一景象撕碎了爱情的神秘感，揭示了一个受生理冲动支配的男性身体。对她来说，这个实验证明了他们之间不存在“填满我们整个存在的”“真爱”：“这不是爱，而只是一段‘情事’。我们在天性上是如此不同，以至于我们没有真正的精神亲近感，没有真正的精神亲密，也没有那种直冲头顶、点燃身体的激情。那它是什么呢？对他来说，是对‘需要’的满足；对我来说，是‘幻想的游戏’。”阿廖沙反过来蔑视她“关于爱情及其表达方式的过时观念”。他责备她缺乏政治意识，还把试验农场的工作问题归咎于她。与此同时，他拒绝讨论他的党内活动，从而显示出他对她这个非共产党人和阶级异己的不信任。至少有一次，她觉得自己像是在受审，因为他向她盘问一名同事的下落，并让她对他撒谎。总而言之，她对与一个党务工作定义了生活各方面的共产党人结合感到巨大的怀疑。

关于这段关系的多种失调，最引人注目的是德尼谢夫斯卡娅对它们的解读。她沉思道，阿廖沙无法培养“个人生活”或去“爱”，不仅指向他个人，也指向他整个历史世代——即新兴“新人”一代的缺陷。这一代人是“命运多舛”的，因为历史规律要求他们为建设共产主义世界而牺牲个人生活。由于被国家事务压得筋疲力尽，他们的心理发展不能不受到损害。由于历史的必然性，过渡时期的“年轻一代”——这些建设新社会却尚未能生活于其中的年轻人——是自我牺牲的存在，他们的生活“在某种程度上是不真实的”，因为他们缺乏成熟的个人灵魂。正如她在给阿廖沙的信中所说：“历史‘注定’你要进行匆忙且无休止的工作……你不该为此受到指责。但知道你被历史‘注定’了这样的命运，让我感到难过。”

With great anticipation she awaited his next visit to Voronezh, in February 1930. Alyosha stayed only two days, but that was long enough to shatter her expectations. As she confided to the diary, she had wanted to see him, for the first time, totally naked, so as to experience his feelings for her directly and totally, but instead the sight tore apart the mystery of love, revealing a male body governed by physiological urges. To her the experiment proved that there existed between them no “real love,” “which would fill our entire being”: “This is not love, but just a ‘liaison.’ We are so different in our nature that we don’t have a real spiritual closeness, and we don’t have real, spiritual intimacy, and there’s no passion that would go to one’s head and set our bodies on fire. What is it then? For him—the satisfaction of a ‘need,’ and for me a ‘game of the imagination.’” Alyosha, in turn, disdained her “old-fashioned notions of love, and of how to express it.” He reproached her for her lack of political consciousness, and he also blamed her for work problems on the experimental farm. Meanwhile he refused to discuss his party activities, thereby showing his distrust toward her as a non-Communist and a class alien. At least once she felt subjected to a veritable interrogation, as he questioned her about the whereabouts of a colleague and made her lie to him. All in all, she had major doubts about a union with a Communist whose commitment to the party defined all aspects of his life.

The most remarkable thing about the multiple dysfunctions that characterized this relationship is Denisevskaya’s interpretation of them. Alyosha’s inability to cultivate a “personal life” or to “love,” she mused, pointed to a defect not only of him individually but of his entire historical generation—the generation of the emerging “new man.” This generation was “doomed” because the laws of history required that they sacrifice their personal lives for the building of the Communist world. Strained to exhaustion by affairs of state, their psychological development could not but be crippled. By historical necessity, the “young generation” of the transition period, the young men and women who built—but could not yet inhabit—the new society, were self-sacrificing beings whose lives were “somehow not authentic,” because they lacked developed individual souls. As she said in a letter to Alyosha, “History has ‘doomed’ you to rushed and ceaseless work . . . You should not be blamed for this. But knowing that you are ‘doomed’ makes me sad.”

这一解读告诉她，她想与他建立心理关系的愿望是错误的。期待他们灵魂的精神交流是一个历史上不可能实现的奢求。他是一个“现代风格的人”，没有成熟的灵魂，对他来说，她所理解的爱是毫无意义的。历史理性的声音有能力定位甚至消解她的心理需求：“没有阿廖沙的信。有时我极度想念他，但当我在晚上读报纸时，我就能理解他的沉默。”读报纸——历史进步的记录——提醒她阿廖沙的使命，并压抑了她那些过时的欲望。根据这种历史解释，她清楚地意识到，很多时候她都误解了阿廖沙。她现在明白了，她曾认为陈腐且阻碍个人表达的那些党派用语，其实就是他的个人语言，即现代社会那种清醒而写实的语言。

历史不仅解释了阿廖沙和年轻一代，也解释了她自己。她也是一种历史类型，悬浮在旧与新之间：“我的观点、我的行为和我的生活总是让我与老一代隔绝。与此同时，我没有力量和健康来承受新一代的生活节奏。”这种历史困境也解释了她的孤独生活：在意识形态上远离老一代而亲近年轻人，但在生理上（年龄、健康、体力）又无法与年轻人并肩作战。但她从作为新一代的先驱中获得了安慰。她一生都在为这年轻的一代工作——她补充说，这也解释了为什么她对阿廖沙的感情带有如此多的母性色彩。

This interpretation showed her that she had been mistaken in wanting to form a psychological relationship with him. To expect a spiritual communion of their souls was to make a historically impossible demand. He was a “man of modern style” who had no developed soul and for whom love, as she understood it, was meaningless. The voice of historical reason had the power to situate, even dissolve, her psychological needs: “No letters from Alyosha. There are times when I miss him extremely, but when I read the newspaper in the evening I understand his silence.” Reading the paper, the record of history’s progress, reminded her of Alyosha’s mission and subdued her anachronistic desires. In light of this historical explanation, it became clear to her that she had misunderstood Alyosha much of the time. She now understood that his party idiom, which she had considered clichéd and an obstacle to personal expression, was in fact his personal language, the sober and factual language of modern times.

History explained not just Alyosha and the young generation, but herself as well. She too was a historical type, suspended between old and new: “My views, my behavior, and my life have always kept me apart from the older generation. At the same time, I don’t have the strength and health to endure the pace of life of the new generation.” This historical predicament also explained her lonely existence: ideologically removed from the old generation and close to the young, yet biologically (in terms of age, health, strength) incapable of marching with the young. But she drew comfort from being a harbinger of the new generation. All her life she had been working for this young generation—and this, she added, also explained why her feelings for Alyosha carried so many motherly overtones.

德尼谢夫斯卡娅并不是唯一以这种方式反思年轻一代的人。那个时期的小说、医学刊物和公开辩论都讨论了革命计划中拆除旧生活形式、构建新秩序所固有的非凡压力和多重断裂。在过时的旧世界和尚未出现的新世界之间的过渡期，居住着一代自我牺牲的年轻共产主义男女。这一代人的文学表现与后来社会主义现实主义散文中和谐、情感和身体完整的英雄形象形成了鲜明对比。与他们在历史进程中的辩证角色一致，20世纪20年代的英雄是片面的、禁欲的、自我否定的战士型人物。他们满身尘土和伤痕，经常患病，无法建立个人关系。他们不代表社会主义社会的“新人”，而是作为其先驱、祖先或教育者。
德尼谢夫斯卡娅也将这种失衡一代的产生归因于历史演进规律。在某种程度上，她对阿廖沙的描述也回响了亚历山德拉·柯伦泰的著作，后者曾将“新女性”称为“过渡类型”，过着不完整的生活，但通过致力于构建完美和完整的未来而获得认可。
即使德尼谢夫斯卡娅承认对阿廖沙这样“命运为历史所注定”的人有着对真爱的过时渴望，她对亲密爱情作为衡量个人关系标准的强调表明，仍有一些“个人主义”和“资产阶级”的自我观念是她（尚未）准备放弃的。

Denisevskaya was not alone in reflecting on the young generation in such terms. Novels, medical publications, and public debates of the period discussed the extraordinary stress and the manifold disruptions inherent in the revolutionary project of tearing down old forms of life while constructing the new order. The interim between the outdated old world and the not-yet-present new one was inhabited by a generation of young, self-sacrificing Communist men and women. Literary representations of this generation differed starkly from the harmonious, emotionally and physically integrated hero who would come to characterize later socialist realist prose. Consistent with their dialectical role in history’s progression, the heroes from the 1920s were one-sided ascetic and self-renouncing warrior types. They were covered with dust and wounds, often sick, and unable to form personal relationships. They did not embody the “new man” of socialist society but acted as its precursor, progenitor, or educator.

Denisevskaya too saw the laws of historical progression as responsible for the creation of this unbalanced generation. In part her characterization of Alyosha also echoed the writings of Alexandra Kollontai, who had spoken of the “new woman” as a “transitional type,” living an incomplete life but receiving validation from her dedication to constructing the perfect and complete future.

Even if Denisevskaya admitted to an anachronistic yearning for real love from a “historically doomed” person like Alyosha, her very emphasis on intimate love as the measure of a personal relationship suggested that there were certain “individualist” and “bourgeois” notions of self that she was not (yet) ready to forgo.

最终，这段产生过如此多希望、反思和斗争的与阿廖沙的结合，结果正如德尼谢夫斯卡娅忧郁地指出的那样，只是一场短暂的“秋天童话”，指的是1929年的秋天，可能也指的是她自己生命的秋天。这段关系的结局带有明显的讽刺意味，但她却没察觉。长期以来，她一直拒绝阿廖沙的追求，担心他的文化落后会让她难堪，但她现在得出的结论是，他们在政治上是不相容的：人们会怀疑她与一个“有着光明前景的年轻党务工作者”的关系中带有“某种自私、利己的底色……我还记得你在不同时间提到的关于普通人讨好党员的各种评论。我感到你的党员身份和你的年轻是我们之间一堵无法逾越的墙，由生活条件所造，而我从这堵墙边退缩了。”分手后德尼谢夫斯卡娅陷入了孤独和绝望，但在疗养院一个月的逗留帮助她认识到了这段关系的好处。其一，阿廖沙教会了她一些表达性欲的方式，让她接受了以前被压抑的“生理冲动”。更重要的是，她开始理解个人之爱（无论是心理上还是生理上定义的）的微不足道，以及在它之外开启的广阔平原——对集体的升华之爱：“事实证明，性吸引只是生活中极小极小的一部分；爱是次要的情感；集体消除了孤独……我在马克思主义中发现了一个新世界。我带着深厚的兴趣阅读。”

In the end the union with Alyosha, which generated so much hope, reflection, and struggle, turned out to be but a brief “autumn fairy tale,” as Denisevskaya noted wistfully, referring to the autumn of 1929 and possibly also to the autumn of her own life. There was a distinct irony to the ending of their relationship, but it was lost on her. While for a long time she had rejected Alyosha’s advances, fearing that his cultural backwardness would embarrass her, she now concluded that they were politically incompatible: people would suspect that there was “some sort of a selfish, egoistic lining” in her relations with a “young party worker with a potentially brilliant future . . . I also remembered various remarks you made at different times about ordinary people in-gratiating themselves with party members. And I felt your party membership and your youth to be an insurmountable wall between us, created by the conditions of life, and I step back from this wall.” Following the break-up Denisevskaya fell back into loneliness and despair, but a month-long stay in a sanatorium helped her recognize the benefits of the relationship. For one, Alyosha had taught her a lesson or two  in sexual expression, allowing her to accept her previously repressed “physiological urges.” More important yet, she had begun to understand the low significance of personal love, whether psychologically or physiologically defined, and the enormous plain opening up beyond it—sublimated love for the collective: “It turns out that sexual attraction is just a tiny, minuscule part of life; love is a secondary feeling; and loneliness is destroyed by the collective . . . I have discovered a new world for me in Marxism. I read with deep interest.”

德尼谢夫斯卡娅一直渴望生命中有一个男人，然而通过他，她发现了集体。由于无法建立深刻的个人纽带，她意识到了同志式的、集体主义之爱的前景。而那位帮助重新引导她的爱的老师，正是她以前的学生阿廖沙本人。他现在已经离开了，但在离开之前，他已让苏维埃思想在她心中孕育，这是一种认为个人生活应从属于集体生活，并将集体视为个人幸福和成就的终极衡量标准的自我观。

Denisevskaya had longed for a man in her life, and yet through him, she had discovered the collective. Unable to forge a profound personal bond, she became aware of the prospect of comradely, collectivist love. And the teacher who had helped redirect her love was her former student Alyosha himself. He was now gone, but before leaving he had impregnated her with the Soviet idea, a view of the self that held personal life to be subordinate to the life of the collective and regarded the collective as the ultimate measure of individual happiness and fulfillment.
